The 2026 North Carolina elections will be held in the state of North Carolina on November 3, 2026, alongside the nationwide midterm elections. Elections will be held for a U.S. Senate seat as well as all 14 of the state's U.S. House of Representatives seats, all seats in the North Carolina Senate and House of Representatives, as well as judicial and local elections. Candidate qualifying for the primaries was held from December 1 to December 19, 2025.[1] Primary elections were held on March 3, 2026, and runoff elections will be held on May 12.[2]

A swing state, North Carolina frequently votes for both Republicans and Democrats statewide.[3][4] Democrats have controlled the governorship since 2017.[5] Partisan control of the Council of State is divided, with Democrats controlling the offices of Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General, Secretary of State, and Superintendent of Public Instruction, and Republicans controlling the offices of Auditor, Commissioner of Agriculture, Commissioner of Labor, and Commissioner of Insurance.[6] Democrats have not won a statewide federal election in North Carolina since 2008, when Barack Obama narrowly carried the state over John McCain and Kay Hagan unseated Elizabeth Dole in the U.S. Senate.[7]

In 2024, North Carolina saw mixed election results. Donald Trump carried the state over Kamala Harris by 3.2%.[8] Following redistricting, Republicans picked up three Democratic-held seats in the United States House of Representatives.[9] In the race for governor, Democratic attorney general Josh Stein defeated Lieutenant Governor Mark Robinson in a landslide.[10][11] Democrats flipped control of the Lieutenant Governor and Superintendent of Public Instruction offices, and Republicans flipped control of the State Auditor's office.[6]

United States Senate

[edit]
Main article: 2026 United States Senate election in North Carolina

Incumbent Republican senator Thom Tillis, who was re-elected with 48.7% of the vote in 2020, is retiring.[12]

Former Democratic governor Roy Cooper ran for the Democratic nomination.[13] Former Democratic representative Wiley Nickel originally announced he was running for the Democratic nomination, but withdrew in July 2025.[14] Former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley and attorney Don Brown ran for the Republican nomination.[15][16] Roy Cooper and Michael Whatley won their respective races during the primaries, and will face each other in the general election.[17]

United States House of Representatives

[edit]
Main article: 2026 United States House of Representatives elections in North Carolina

All 14 of North Carolina's seats in the United States House of Representatives are up for election in 2026.[18]

Ten seats are currently held by Republicans, and four are held by Democrats.[18]

State House of Representatives

[edit]
Main article: 2026 North Carolina House of Representatives election

All 120 seats in the North Carolina House of Representatives are up for election in 2026. North Carolina state representatives serve two year terms, with the last election being in 2024.[20]

Republicans currently hold 71 seats in the State House, one seat short of a supermajority, and Democrats hold 49 seats following the 2024 elections.[21]

State Senate

[edit]
Main article: 2026 North Carolina Senate election

All 50 seats in the North Carolina Senate are up for election in 2026. North Carolina state senators serve two year terms.[22]

Judicial elections

[edit]
Main article: 2026 North Carolina judicial elections

One seat on the North Carolina Supreme Court and three seats on the North Carolina Court of Appeals are up for election in 2026.[23][24] Supreme Court justices serve eight year terms.[25]

Incumbent Democratic Supreme Court justice Anita Earls is running for re-election to the North Carolina Supreme Court.[23] She is being challenged by Republican state representative Sarah Stevens.[26]

Ballot measures

[edit]
Further information: 2026 North Carolina Require Voter Identification Amendment
This section needs to be updated. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. (May 2026)

One statewide ballot measure is scheduled to be on the November 2026 ballot. Senate Bill 921 was passed by the North Carolina Legislature in December 2024 and would require voters to provide photo identification regardless of the method in which they intend to vote.[27] As it amends the North Carolina Constitution, it will require at least 50% of North Carolina voters to approve of the measure for it to become law.[28]
